analysis.one_liner: Replaces Medicare's private drug plans with a no-premium government benefit and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices directly.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after introduction it sat in two House committees and its subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have thrown out the Medicare prescription drug benefit created in 2003, which is run through private insurance plans with monthly premiums, deductibles, and gaps in coverage. In its place it would have created a Medicare-run drug benefit with no premium, no deductible, 10% coinsurance, and a $1,500 yearly cap on out-of-pocket costs, with the government negotiating maximum drug prices directly with manufacturers. It also would have allowed cheaper drug imports from Canada, repealed a fund that subsidizes private Medicare Advantage plans, and repealed health savings accounts. It was referred to two House committees in November 2005, sent to a Health Subcommittee the next month, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million Medicare beneficiaries of the time, who would have gotten drug coverage without paying a monthly premium or deductible, with coinsurance capped at 10% and total out-of-pocket drug spending capped at $1,500 a year, and with much lower copays ($1 generic, $3 brand-name) for people earning under 150% of the poverty line. Enrollees would have been enrolled automatically, with no penalty for joining late.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries paying high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: The replacement benefit has no monthly premium, no annual deductible, 10% coinsurance, and a $1,500 annual out-of-pocket limit, with reduced copays for lower-income beneficiaries [S2, S3].

It directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate maximum prices with drug manufacturers, and requires pharmacy contractors to negotiate prices lower than those maxima and pass the savings to beneficiaries [S3].
It would let qualifying individuals, not just pharmacists and wholesalers, import prescription drugs from Canada, restoring rules rolled back by the 2003 Medicare law [S2].

It repeals provisions of the 2003 law that subsidize private Medicare Advantage plans (the Regional Plan Stabilization Fund and the Comparative Cost Adjustment program), phases private plan payments toward the fee-for-service rate, and bars rules that would push beneficiaries out of traditional Medicare [S2, S3].

It guarantees participating pharmacies a role in the program, including dispensing fees, rural access bonus payments, and quick electronic reimbursement, and it makes payments to employers who maintain retiree drug coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices would be capped by government negotiation and undercut by Canadian imports; private Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers, whose role would shrink sharply; and federal taxpayers, who would fund a new Medicare Prescription Drug Trust Fund covering a benefit with no premiums or deductibles.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, insurers, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The benefit design is expensive: eliminating premiums, deductibles, and most cost-sharing while capping out-of-pocket spending at $1,500 creates large, open-ended federal spending through a new trust fund funded by appropriations [S3].

The bill shields key government decisions from challenge: the Secretary's contract awards, regional map, therapeutic classes, and breakthrough-drug determinations would not be subject to administrative or judicial review [S3].

It lets the Secretary waive standard conflict-of-interest rules when awarding the pharmacy-administration contracts, a carve-out that could open the door to the same industry entanglement the bill otherwise polices [S3].

A good-faith objection from supporters of the 2003 law: replacing competing private drug plans with government-negotiated contracts removes plan choice, and critics argued government price-setting could reduce manufacturers' incentive to develop new drugs — a concern the bill only partially answers with its 'breakthrough drug' provisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the gains are large and concrete: no premium, no deductible, a hard $1,500 out-of-pocket cap, and lower prices through negotiation and importation. The cost is a substantial new federal obligation and the loss of private-plan choice, and the bill has real design flaws — unreviewable agency decisions and a conflict-of-interest waiver in contracting. The core trade-off is genuine, but the bill's benefits to seniors would clearly outweigh its costs for most beneficiaries; the open question is the federal price tag.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2005, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, sent to a Health Subcommittee in December, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on November 18, 2005 [S1, S5].
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
On December 16, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health; no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].
The bill drew five cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and the private insurance plans created by the 2003 Medicare drug law came out ahead: the private Part D structure — premiums, deductibles, and a ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices — stayed in place, and beneficiaries kept paying their share of drug costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Medicare drug plans

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the private Medicare drug benefit with a Medicare-run benefit and to allow drug importation from Canada.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action beyond sending it to the Subcommittee on Health.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received a split referral covering its jurisdiction and took no recorded action on the bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration; no action on the bill occurs after the subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats; the bill sat in committees controlled by the Republican majority and never advanced.

industries.note: The bill directs the government to negotiate maximum prices for Medicare-covered drugs and lets individuals import drugs from Canada, both of which cut into drug-company revenue on products seniors buy. Its interest in stopping the bill ran against beneficiaries' interest in cheaper drugs.

industries.industry: Part D drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill repeals the private-plan drug benefit created in 2003 and replaces it with government-contracted pharmacy administrators chosen by competitive bidding, eliminating the industry's role as the middleman for Medicare drug coverage.

The bill repeals the Regional Plan Stabilization Fund and the Comparative Cost Adjustment program, phases private-plan payments toward the standard fee-for-service rate, and imposes new drug-benefit requirements on the plans.
The bill keeps payments flowing to employer group plans that maintain retiree drug coverage at least as generous as the new benefit, reducing pressure on employers to drop that coverage.
Pharmacies meeting program standards are guaranteed participation agreements, plus dispensing fees, prompt electronic reimbursement, and rural bonus payments.
